h1: The 5 Best Inverter Microwaves of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: five inverter microwaves from Panasonic, Toshiba and LG, compared by capacity, footprint and price, from 1.3 to 1.6 cu. ft.
summary: The Panasonic NN-SN76LS is our best overall, a 1.6 cu. ft. cyclonic inverter model. The LG Smart Inverter is the pick for sensor cooking in a slightly smaller cavity, the Toshiba ML-EM45PIT adds a smart sensor, and the Toshiba Flatbed at 1.3 cu. ft. is the cheapest way into inverter cooking.
intro: An inverter microwave does not blast at full power and then switch off; it delivers a steady stream of lower power. That matters most for defrosting and reheating, where on-off pulses leave frozen centers and rubbery edges. The mistake most buyers make is paying the inverter premium and then using it only for popcorn.

We reviewed eight listings and kept five whose spec sheets explicitly state inverter technology. The Sharp and two Panasonic models were left out because their listings do not name an inverter. This is a paper ranking from the specs, not bench work.

products.name: Panasonic NN-SN76LS 1.6 cu.ft Cyclonic Inverter Countertop Microwave
products.verdict: A 1.6 cu. ft. cyclonic inverter model with a clear spec sheet.
products.description:
The Panasonic NN-SN76LS has a 1.6 cu. ft. cavity and is described as a cyclonic inverter model. The exterior measures 21.88 inches wide, 19.44 inches deep and 11.94 inches high, which is a standard footprint for its capacity.

It ranks first because it combines the largest cavity of the group with the strongest inverter wording. The LG gives up some capacity at 1.5 cu. ft. for sensor cooking.

Buy it for family reheating. The caveat is the $200 to $500 price, which is the bucket every pick here shares except the Flatbed.
products.skipIf: You have a very small counter.

products.name: LG Countertop Microwave
products.verdict: Smart Inverter plus sensor cooking in 1.5 cu. ft.
products.description:
The LG countertop microwave has a 1.5 cu. ft. cavity, Smart Inverter and sensor cooking, with exterior dimensions of 21.44 by 12.13 by 16.19 inches.

It ranks second because the Panasonic offers 0.1 cu. ft. more room, while the LG's 16.19 inch depth is more compact.

It suits kitchens where depth is limited. The caveat is the same $200 to $500 price.
products.idealFor: Shallower counters that still need an inverter.

products.name: TOSHIBA ML-EM45PIT(SS) Countertop Microwave Oven with Inverter
products.verdict: Inverter, smart sensor and auto defrost in 1.6 cu. ft.
products.description:
The Toshiba ML-EM45PIT offers 1.6 cu. ft. of capacity with inverter technology, a smart sensor and auto defrost.

It ranks third because it matches the Panasonic on capacity but its listing gives fewer dimensions.

Good for defrost-heavy cooks. The caveat is the same price bucket as the Panasonic.
products.skipIf: You want a stated exterior size.

products.name: TOSHIBA Countertop Microwave Oven with Inverter Technology
products.verdict: Another 1.6 cu. ft. Toshiba with inverter technology.
products.description:
This Toshiba is a 1.6 cu. ft. countertop microwave with inverter technology, in the $200 to $500 bucket.

It ranks fourth because its spec list is thinner than the ML-EM45PIT, which names a smart sensor and auto defrost.

Choose it as a plain inverter option. The caveat is the sparse listing detail.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want inverter without extras.
products.skipIf: You want listed smart sensor features.

products.name: TOSHIBA Flatbed Microwave Oven with Inverter Technology
products.verdict: The only inverter pick in the $100 to $200 bucket.
products.description:
The Toshiba Flatbed has a 1.3 cu. ft. cavity, 1200W and inverter technology, and costs less than the rest at $100 to $200.

It ranks last because the cavity is the smallest of the group, but it undercuts every other inverter pick on cost.

Pick it if you want an inverter on a budget. The caveat is the smaller cavity.
products.skipIf: You cook for a large household.

whatMatters.detail: An inverter delivers steady power instead of pulsing a full-power magnetron on and off. That gives more even defrosting and gentler reheating. Look for the word inverter in the title; the Sharp and two Panasonic models here lacked it.
Capacity in cubic feet is the cavity size. A 1.6 cu. ft. model fits a large dinner plate, while 1.3 cu. ft. is tighter. Check the number against the plate you use.
The exterior size decides whether the unit fits your counter. Add clearance for the door and vents. Look for width, depth and height in the listing.
A sensor measures steam and adjusts cooking time. It helps with reheating without guessing. The LG and Toshiba ML-EM45PIT mention it.
Wattage is raw power, such as the Toshiba Flatbed's 1200W. Higher wattage usually cooks faster. Check it in the title or bullet points.

faq.a: It delivers steady power instead of cycling on and off, which helps even defrosting and reheating.
Assuming every premium microwave has an inverter. Several do not, so look for the word in the title.

faq.q: Is it worth it over a standard model?
faq.a: If you defrost and reheat often, yes. For popcorn only, a cheaper model is fine.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Leave clearance around the vents, plug into a dedicated outlet and place the plate carefully.
Wipe the interior with a damp cloth after steamy foods.

faq.q: Why were Sharp and some Panasonic models left out?
faq.a: Their listings did not state inverter technology.

finalTake: The Panasonic NN-SN76LS is the best all-round inverter microwave. Pick the LG for sensor cooking and a shallow depth, the Toshiba ML-EM45PIT for auto defrost, or the Toshiba Flatbed if budget matters. Match cavity size to your plates first.
